back: Confirming that each outcome is worth the time, effort and money invested. In agile, by short cycles and rapid feedback.
The product owner, by business value, working with stakeholders and customers.
Outputs: the things built. Outcomes: the benefits achieved when they are used.
It confirms value; it surfaces hidden work (deployment, documentation, compliance); it reduces risk.
Must have, should have, could have, will not have.

front: Which MoSCoW items are dropped first?
back: Could have. Must-have items are never dropped.
Classifies features as basic (expected), performance (more is better) or delighter (unexpected).
Expected by customers. Its absence causes dissatisfaction; its presence goes unnoticed.
Unexpected. Its presence delights; its absence is not missed.
One ordered list with no ties. Needs a single decision owner.
A 2 × 2 grid plotting each item's impact against its effort. Shows quick wins.
What it costs to wait: prioritizes by time-sensitivity and economic impact.
Cost of delay ÷ job size. The highest score goes first.
Stakeholders spend a fixed budget of money or points on the items they want. Reveals true preferences.
Focused on learning: the smallest version that lets the team test assumptions and get feedback from real users.
Focused on release: the smallest version with enough features to be offered to the market and deliver value customers will pay for.
The smallest deliverable piece of functionality that has value to the business.
MVP is for learning. MMP is for selling.
An event in which the team presents completed, working product to stakeholders to get feedback and validate progress.

front: How often to demonstrate working product
back: At least once every two weeks, as a general guideline.

front: Who accepts or declines stories at a demonstration?
back: The product owner.

front: Release on a cadence vs on demand
back: Cadence: at regular intervals, giving a predictable rhythm. On demand: whenever an increment is worth releasing.
Delivering feature increments to customers immediately, using small batches and automation.
The product owner, once the definition of done is met.
The deferred cost of work not done at an earlier point in the product's life. Makes later changes slower.

front: How is technical debt paid down?
back: By refactoring: improving the design without changing the expected behavior.
Continuous: stakeholders see and comment on working product every iteration, and status is kept visible on information radiators.

front: Factors that affect backlog order besides value
back: Risk (do risky items early), dependencies between items, and effort.
